title: Determination of the adsorption isotherms and transport diffusivities of gases in mixtures inside zeolitic crystals using Infra-Red Micro-imaging
author: Carter, Tezel, et al.

steps.title: Place crystal in quartz cell
steps.instruction: Insert the zeolite crystal into a quartz sample cell, connect the cell to the experimental manifold, and place the cell inside the portable tubular furnace.

steps.title: Evacuate and dry crystal
steps.instruction: Open valves V‑101 to V‑109 and evacuate the system with vacuum pump P‑101 while heating the furnace to 400 °C–450 °C (typically 450 °C) to remove moisture; maintain vacuum < 10⁻⁴ mbar. After evacuation, remove the quartz cell from the furnace and place it on the IRM stage, then close valves V‑101 to V‑109.

steps.title: Load gas into reservoir R‑102
steps.instruction: For pure‑gas uptake, open V‑101, V‑102 and V‑104 and fill reservoir R‑102 from the gas cylinder until the desired maximum pressure is read on pressure gauge P1; then add extra gas to compensate for the system volume at that pressure and close the three valves. For gas‑mixture uptake at room temperature, introduce the second gas cylinder, re‑evacuate the process lines by opening V‑101, V‑106 and V‑108, then close them; set the partial pressures to obtain the required molar composition (e.g., 15 % CO₂ / 85 % N₂). All gases have 99.998 % purity (Sigma, Germany).

steps.title: Acquire reference IR spectrum
steps.instruction: Operate the IR microscope (IRM) in optical mode and focus the IR laser on the zeolite crystal; switch to IR transmittance mode and record the transmittance spectrum of the crystal to serve as the reference spectrum.

steps.title: Transfer gas to measurement cell
steps.instruction: Open valves V‑103 and V‑105 to allow gas from R‑102 to fill reservoir R‑101, then slowly open V‑104 until the pressure measured by gauge P3 reaches the target (e.g., 10.2 kPa for a 0 → 10 kPa step, the extra 0.2 kPa compensates the sample‑cell volume). Close V‑104.

steps.title: Apply pressure step and record spectra
steps.instruction: Set the FTIR to continuously acquire IR transmittance spectra of both bulk gas phase and crystal while quickly opening valve V‑109 to impose the pressure step; continue recording until the spectra no longer change, indicating equilibrium.

steps.title: Determine adsorbed amount – bulk and crystal
steps.instruction: a) With the FTIR, record the equilibrium transmittance spectra of bulk gas and crystal (step 4.1). b) Switch the IRM back to optical mode, move the quartz cell so the laser focuses on a region without crystal, switch to transmittance mode and record the bulk‑gas‑only spectrum (step 4.2). c) Analyze the equilibrium spectra using both the crystal reference (step 3.1) and the bulk‑gas reference just obtained. d) Return the IRM to optical mode, reposition the laser on the crystal, and close valve V‑109 (step 4.3).

substeps.instruction: Record equilibrium spectra of bulk gas and crystal.
Acquire bulk‑gas‑only spectrum by focusing on empty region of the cell.
Re‑focus on crystal and close V‑109.

steps.title: Repeat pressure steps
steps.instruction: Repeat steps 3 through 7 for every pressure step of interest (e.g., 0 → 10 kPa, 10 → 20 kPa, … up to 250 kPa).

steps.title: Regenerate crystal at high temperature
steps.instruction: Place the crystal in the quartz cell, evacuate to < 10⁻⁴ mbar, heat in the furnace to 450 °C at 5 °C min⁻¹, hold for 11 h, then cool at the same rate to room temperature.

steps.title: Perform uptake experiments for a mixture
steps.instruction: Prepare the specified CO₂/N₂ mixture (e.g., 15 % CO₂ / 85 % N₂) and conduct gas‑uptake measurements at 32 ± 2 °C for pressure steps of 0 → 100 kPa in 10 kPa increments and 100 → 250 kPa in 25 kPa increments; pure N₂ is not measured because it does not absorb IR light.

steps.title: Regenerate crystal at room temperature
steps.instruction: After a mixture series, evacuate the crystal to < 10⁻⁴ mbar at room temperature to remove adsorbed species.

steps.title: Repeat for additional mixtures
steps.instruction: Repeat the sequence “perform uptake experiments” (step 9) and “regenerate at room temperature” (step 10) for gas mixtures of 30 %/70 %, 50 %/50 %, 70 %/30 %, 85 %/15 % CO₂/N₂, and finally 100 % CO₂.

steps.title: Record crystal dimensions
steps.instruction: Note that the silicalite crystal is cuboid with height 510 µm, width 490 µm, and length 1200 µm; these dimensions are used in diffusion‑analysis calculations.

steps.title: Analyze IR data
steps.instruction: Convert transmittance spectra I to absorbance A by A = log(I₀/I) using the reference spectrum I₀; integrate absorbance peaks between 3550 cm⁻¹ and 3740 cm⁻¹ for CO₂; generate a calibration curve (absorbance vs. amount adsorbed) using literature isotherm values at 32 °C (Sips model); calculate adsorption isotherms and transport diffusivities by fitting the relative uptake versus time data to analytical diffusion expressions (slab, sphere, cylinder) from Crank, performing regression analysis to obtain diffusivity values.

substeps.instruction: Create calibration curve using known CO₂ loadings.
Fit uptake curves to diffusion models to extract diffusivities.

description: This method has been validated using a crystal of silicalite with pure CO2 gas, and gas mixtures composed of CO2 and N2. In this investigation, the silicalite crystal was cuboid shaped, and had height, width, and length dimensions of 510 µm, 490 µm, and 1200 µm, respectively. This crystal was fabricated according to a similar method to the one published by Kida et al using quartz as the silica source [6]. The CO2 and N2 gases that were used for pure gas and gas mixture experiments had purities of 99.998%, and were purchased from Sigma (Schnelldorf, Germany). Adsorption isotherms and transport diffusivities were found for CO2 but not N2 since it does not absorb IR light, and so cannot be detected using IRM. These results have been published elsewhere [7]. Isotherms for pure CO2 and silicalite determined using other methods have been published by others [8], [9], [10], [11], which are in agreement with the isotherms generated in this study, and confirm that this method is reliable. As a result, the binary adsorption isotherms for CO2 can also be considered reliable since their IR absorbance spectra is distinct from that of N2. Order of experiments and crystal regeneration conditions for silicalite and mixtures composed of CO2/N2 were as follows:I.The zeolite crystal was first regenerated by removing all adsorbed species from its structure under a vacuum pressure of less than 10−4 mbar at a temperature of 450°C for 11 hours as described in step 1 of the experimental method section. Heating and cooling temperature rates of 5°C per minute were used.II.A gas mixture composed of 15% / 85% CO2 / N2 was prepared, and gas uptake and amounts adsorbed at equilibrium were investigated for CO2 at pressure steps of 10 kPa from 0 to 100 kPa, and then pressure steps of 25 kPa from 100 kPa to 250 kPa.
